title: NEB Class 11 English — Critical Thinking — 2024
subject: english
source: NEB Grade 11 Model Questions / NEB Past Papers 2020-2024

questions.question: What is critical thinking? Explain any three of its key skills with examples.
questions.solution:
**Critical thinking** is disciplined, evidence-based reasoning instead of accepting claims at face value.

**Skills:** (1) **Analysis** — breaking an argument into premises and conclusion. (2) **Evaluation** — testing evidence quality (a viral health claim vs a peer-reviewed trial). (3) **Inference** — drawing warranted conclusions (wet streets → it rained, barring alternatives).
questions.knowledgeNote: Bloom's ladder (remember → create) places evaluation and creation at the top — exams increasingly target those rungs.

questions.question: Distinguish between fact and opinion with two examples of each.
questions.solution:
**Fact** is verifiable: 'Mt. Everest is 8,848.86 m high.' 'Water boils at 100°C at sea level.'

**Opinion** expresses judgement: 'Pokhara is Nepal's most beautiful city.' 'Online classes are better than physical ones.'

Test: can evidence settle it? Yes → fact; no → opinion.
questions.knowledgeNote: Editorials blend both — spotting which sentence is which is the core critical-reading move.

questions.question: What are premises and conclusions in an argument? Identify them in: 'All students must wear uniforms since uniforms reduce economic discrimination.'
questions.solution:
**Premises** are the supporting reasons; the **conclusion** is the claim they support (flagged by 'therefore, so, since, because').

**Premise:** 'uniforms reduce economic discrimination.' **Conclusion:** 'All students must wear uniforms.'

Critical check: does the premise really entail the conclusion, or are cheaper alternatives (dress codes, subsidies) ignored?
questions.knowledgeNote: 'Since/because' introduce premises; 'therefore/so' introduce conclusions — indicator words map arguments instantly.

questions.question: What is a logical fallacy? Explain ad hominem and hasty generalisation with one example of each.
questions.solution:
A **fallacy** is reasoning that looks valid but isn't.

**Ad hominem:** attacking the person, not the claim — 'Don't trust his tax plan; he failed math.' **Hasty generalisation:** leaping from tiny samples — 'Two tourists were rude, so all tourists are rude.'
questions.knowledgeNote: Strawman (distorting the opponent's view) completes the big-three fallacy set for this unit.

questions.question: Write any four criteria for evaluating the credibility of an information source.
questions.solution: (1) **Authority** — qualified author/publisher? (2) **Evidence** — data and citations, or bare claims? (3) **Currency** — recent enough for the topic? (4) **Objectivity** — balanced or pushing an agenda? (+ Purpose: inform vs sell.)
questions.knowledgeNote: Lateral reading — checking what OTHER reputable sites say about a source — beats judging any site by its own design.

questions.question: Distinguish between observation and inference with an example.
questions.solution:
**Observation** reports direct senses: 'The classroom floor is wet.' **Inference** explains it: '…so the roof must be leaking (or someone spilled water).'

Observations are checkable facts; inferences are best-guess explanations — science advances by testing inferences against new observations.
questions.knowledgeNote: Multiple inferences can fit one observation — listing alternatives before concluding is the critical habit.
